content:
#1 As I mentioned in my “new member” post (I don’t know how to do fancy references to other posts yet), I am looking for a notion of “remainder” in category theory.

I’m describing a “system behavior” and a map of that behavior to the behavior of a “component” of the system. The question at hand is: what is the best description I can find of the behavior of the other components?

Because a composition of components (and synchronization between) them, in my category leads to a “jointly monic family” of maps from the system behavior to the behavior of the components, I could therefore say that I’m looking for the “smallest” component that allows me to form a “jointly monic pair” with the map into the “known” component.

I got to this definition at first:

  • given a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a “remainder” of fff is any object ZZZ for which there exists a map g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z such that (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic, and in addition it holds that for any other g′:X→Z′g' : X \rightarrow Z'g′:X→Z′ such that (f,g′)(f,g')(f,g′) is jointly monic, there is a unique k:Z→Z′k : Z \rightarrow Z'k:Z→Z′ such that kg=g′\mathrm{kg} = g'kg=g′.

I though it was a rather natural notion, but have not found references to it yet.

Mike Shulman and David Roberts already responded with two questions:

1) can I give an example of whether such a remainder can exist at all? He didn’t think it would exist for Set.

2) Isn’t it a trivial notion? If you take Y=XY = XY=X, the identity might do the job.

As to 1)… I’m going to think about it. I think I have an example in the category of prefix orders, on which I just posted a page, but I still need to check it. (Apologies for asking the question before doing my homework… but sometimes you can spend hours figuring out what other people already know ;-)

As to 2)… shoot… that is a suggestion I overlooked. In my own examples there are often “smaller” candidates for YYY than XXX, but they do not seem to come out this way. Intuitively, in Set, the map ggg should not be injective at points where fff is already injective. But the definition still allows that apparently. Back to the drawing board… Any suggestions?
subject: Categorical definition of "division" or "remainder"

content: #2 David is right, btw, about any category and any fff at all: your definition says it is an initial object in some full subcategory of X/CX/\mathcal{C}X/C, so as long as that subcategory contains the initial object of X/CX/\mathcal{C}X/C (namely Z=XZ=XZ=X and g=idXg=\mathrm{id}_Xg=idX​) — and it does — that is also the initial object in the subcategory. I think I was originally trying to solve the problem you actually had in mind of making a map that’s “only injective where fff is not”, and that’s what I thought would not exist. Perhaps what you want is a terminal object of the same category? But look at Set\mathrm{Set}Set first; suppose f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y is the first projection 2×2→22\times 2 \to 22×2→2, where 2={0,1}2=\{0,1\}2={0,1}. What do you want ggg to be? Since f(0,1)=f(0,0)f(0,1)=f(0,0)f(0,1)=f(0,0) and f(1,1)=f(1,0)f(1,1)=f(1,0)f(1,1)=f(1,0), you need ggg to separate those pairs. But if you want ggg to be noninjective “at points where fff is already injective” then presumably you want something like g(0,1)=g(1,1)g(0,1) = g(1,1)g(0,1)=g(1,1) or g(0,1)=g(1,0)g(0,1) = g(1,0)g(0,1)=g(1,0) — but you can’t have both of those, otherwise g(1,0)=g(1,1)g(1,0)=g(1,1)g(1,0)=g(1,1) which isn’nt allowed, and there’s no universal way to pick one but not the other.

content:

Indeed, let’s look at Set first. If f:X→Yf: X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y is the first projection of 2×2→22 \times 2 \rightarrow 22×2→2, then (intuitively) I would like ggg to become the second projection. That would at least be my idea of division within Set… Whenever fff is not an actual projection, it will be a bit tricky to tell what ggg should be, but indeed for projections it should work out in any/most categories.

So, what are we doing really then… I think ggg should split the points that fff equates, but it can identify points that fff distinguishes. Furthermore, ggg should identify “as many points as possible”, and that is where the difficulty starts.

content:
#4 Okay, then let’s look at whether terminal objects work…

Second try: given f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, and object ZZZ is a remainder of fff if there exists a map g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z such that (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic, and for any g′:X→Z′g' : X \rightarrow Z'g′:X→Z′ with (f,g′)(f,g')(f,g′) jointly monic there is a map h:Z′→Zh : Z' \rightarrow Zh:Z′→Z such that hg′=gh g' = ghg′=g.

Notice that I have reversed the direction of hhh but also dropped the uniqueness requirement, because it will give trouble whenever g′g'g′ is non-surjective.

This seems to work for the simple 2×22 \times 22×2 example. It is a standard result that the two projections form a jointly monic pair. Furthermore, any candidate Z′Z'Z′ must at least contain two points in order to distinguish (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) from (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), otherwise (f,g′)(f,g')(f,g′) cannot be jointly monic. Furthermore, the image of g′g'g′ will contain at most 444 points, and the remaining points an be mapped arbitrarily to 222. Simply enumerating the possibilities for images that contain 222,333 or 444 points quickly leads to the conclusion that indeed the second projection is a witness to show that 2×22 \times 22×2 divided by 222 gives 222.

I’ve tried a simple example in my category of prefix orders as well, and it also seems to work there.

Next, I guess I should prove that in general when fff is the first projection of a binary product, ggg is the second projection. Or try a few more examples. And after that, we still have the question whether/when ZZZ is unique…
subject: Categorical definition of "division" or "remainder"

content:
#7 Theorem (using either definition version 2 or 3): If in our category of choice all pushouts exist and all epi’s have sections (the axiom of choice, I believe), then the natural projections of a binary product are each-others remainder.

Proof: Let f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X and g:X×Y→Yg : X \times Y \rightarrow Yg:X×Y→Y be natural projections of X×YX \times YX×Y. It is a standard result that (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic. Furthermore, let g′:X×Y→Zg' : X \times Y \rightarrow Zg′:X×Y→Z be such that (f,g′)(f,g')(f,g′) is jointly monic. Then we can create the pushout g′g'g′ and ggg, given by maps p:Y→Pp : Y \rightarrow Pp:Y→P and q:Z→Pq : Z \rightarrow Pq:Z→P. It is a standard result that ppp and qqq are epimorphisms. Let p′:P→Yp' : P \rightarrow Yp′:P→Y be the section of ppp, then we define h=p′qh = p' qh=p′q and find hg′=p′qg′=p′pg=gh g' = p' q g' = p' p g = ghg′=p′qg′=p′pg=g. So we may conclude that YYY is a remainder of fff, witnessed by ggg.

If I didn’t make any mistakes, in Set the remainders (if they are indeed unique) therefore behave as I would like them to for the time being.

#23 In summary so far, working through the above, how about this:

  • Definition: given f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a map g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F is a fraction of fff if (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic and for any jointly monic pair (f,h)(f,h)(f,h) there exists a kkk such that kh=gk h = gkh=g.

  • Uniqueness theorem: if g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F and g′:X→F′g' : X \rightarrow F'g′:X→F′ are epic fractions of f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, then FFF and F′F'F′ are isomorphic.

    Proof: (I guess this is a standard result for weakly final epis, but I am a real newbe, so I need to do this for my own understanding.) Consider g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F and g′:X→F′g' : X \rightarrow F'g′:X→F′ to be epimorphic fractions of f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y. Then there exist kkk and k′k'k′ such that kg=g′k g = g'kg=g′ and k′g′=gk' g' = gk′g′=g. So 1g=g=k′g′=k′kg1 g = g = k' g' = k' k g1g=g=k′g′=k′kg and because ggg is epic we find k′k=1k' k = 1k′k=1. Similarly, kk′=1k k' = 1kk′=1. Q.E.D.

  • Basic intuition theorem: consider the natural projections f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X and g:X×Y→Yg : X \times Y \rightarrow Yg:X×Y→Y of a product X×YX \times YX×Y, then fff is an epic fraction of ggg and ggg is an epic fraction of fff.

    Proof: that projections are epic is standard, and that the theorem is symmetric is clear, so we only need to prove that ggg is a fraction of fff. How to go about that is not so clear to me. Maybe it is not even true in general, in which case my definition might need more tweaking.

content:
#30 Yes, that might work too, I suppose. (According to kernel you actually mean kernel pair, right? The pullback of fff along itself.)

After a nights sleep, I figured out how to adapt my own definition a bit as well, so now I have two definitions which both seem reasonable (for the time being).

  • Definition 1: Given a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, an object FFF is a fraction of fff if for every g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z with (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) jointly monic, there exists an h:Z→Fh: Z \rightarrow Fh:Z→F such that (f,hg)(f,\mathrm{hg})(f,hg) is jointly monic and hg\mathrm{hg}hg is an epimorphism.
  • Theorem 1: Fractions are unique up-to isomorphism.

Proof: let FFF and F′F'F′ both be fractions of fff. Observe that (f,1)(f,1)(f,1) is jointly monic. Applying the definition of fraction gives us maps g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F and g′:X→F′g' : X \rightarrow F'g′:X→F′ such that (f,g1)(f,g1)(f,g1) and (f,g′1)(f,g'1)(f,g′1) are jointly monic, and g=g1g = g1g=g1 and g′=g′1g' = g'1g′=g′1 are epimorphisms. Applying the definition of fraction again gives us maps hhh and h′h'h′ such that hg=g′\mathrm{hg} = g'hg=g′ and h′g′=gh'g' = gh′g′=g. From this we obtain 1g=g=h′g′=h′hg1g = g = h'g' = h' h g1g=g=h′g′=h′hg, and because ggg is epic, 1=h′h1 = h' h1=h′h. Similarly, 1=hh′1 = h h'1=hh′. So hhh and h′h'h′ are isomorphisms between FFF and F′F'F′.

  • Conjecture: Given a natural projection f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X, if fff has a fraction, then it is isomorphic to YYY.

  • Conjecture: Given a natural projection f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X, we find YYY is a fraction of fff.

And my first quick attempt to formalize Mike’s suggestion, while keeping it ‘comparable’ to the first definition. (I’m not sure if I got the translation into arrows entirely right, please have a look).

  • Definition 2 : Given a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y. Let k,k′:R→Xk,k' : R \rightarrow Xk,k′:R→X be the kernel pair of fff (the pullback of fff over itself). An object FFF is a fraction of fff if there exists an epimorphism g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F for which the kernel pair h,h′:S→Xh,h' : S \rightarrow Xh,h′:S→X (the pullback of ggg over itself) has the property that every m:X→Zm : X \rightarrow Zm:X→Z with hm=h′m\mathrm{hm} = h'mhm=h′m and km=k′m\mathrm{km} = k'mkm=k′m is a monomorphism.

  • Conjecture: Fractions are unique up-to isomorphism.

  • Conjecture: Given a natural projection f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X, if fff has a fraction, then it is isomorphic to YYY.

  • Conjecture: Given a natural projection f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X, we find YYY is a fraction of fff.

I’ll get back later to seeing whether I can prove any of the conjectures, or find conditions under which they can be proven.
subject: Categorical definition of "division" or "remainder"

content:
#31

Definition 2 : Given a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y. Let k,k′:R→Xk,k' : R \rightarrow Xk,k′:R→X be the kernel pair of fff (the pullback of fff over itself). An object FFF is a fraction of fff if there exists an epimorphism g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F for which the kernel pair h,h′:S→Xh,h' : S \rightarrow Xh,h′:S→X (the pullback of ggg over itself) has the property that every m:X→Zm : X \rightarrow Zm:X→Z with hm=h′mh m = h'mhm=h′m and km=k′mk m = k'mkm=k′m is a monomorphism.

Close! But I think the inclusions go the other direction: hm=h′mh m = h' mhm=h′m means that the kernel pair of mmm contains (h,h′)(h,h')(h,h′), not conversely. Also there should be some kind of maximality condition, e.g. that their union in the poset of equivalence relations is the full relation, i.e. they are complements in that poset. Finally, an object in category theory should be equipped with a morphism rather than just be such that a morphism exists (e.g. a cartesian product is equipped with projections A←A×B→BA\leftarrow A\times B \to BA←A×B→B). So if we turn all the equivalence relations into epimorphisms, I would state the definition something like this:

Definition 2: Given a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a fraction of fff is an epimorphism g:X→Fg:X\to Fg:X→F such that (1) if e:X→Ze:X\to Ze:X→Z is an epimorphism such that fff and ggg both factor through it, then eee is an isomorphism; and (2) the pushout of fff and ggg is constant (factors through the terminal object).

However, with this definition as stated, your first conjecture

Fractions are unique up to isomorphism.

is false in complete generality. Consider any lattice PPP as a thin category and let x∈Px\in Px∈P be an object that has more than one distinct complement, i.e. y,y′y,y'y,y′ with x∧y=x∧y′=0x\wedge y = x\wedge y' = 0x∧y=x∧y′=0 and x∨y=x∨y′=1x\vee y = x\vee y' = 1x∨y=x∨y′=1. Then since every morphism in a thin category is epi, 0→y0\to y0→y and 0→y′0\to y'0→y′ are nonisomorphic fractions of 0→x0\to x0→x. This is also a counterexample to your second conjecture, since 0=x×y=x×y′0 = x\times y = x\times y'0=x×y=x×y′.

However, a more reasonable formulation would be to add conditions on the category and/or restrict to some well-behaved subclass of epimorphisms like strong, extremal, or regular ones. Of course it’s still false if you ask for the isomorphism to respect the morphisms from XXX, but absent that condition I don’t yet know the answer (though there could still be an easy one, I haven’t thought about it very hard).

Moreover, your third conjecture:

Given a natural projection f:X×Y→Xf : X \times Y \rightarrow Xf:X×Y→X, we find YYY is a fraction of fff.

is almost true, in good cases. It’s not quite true even in Set\mathrm{Set}Set because X×Y→YX\times Y \to YX×Y→Y may not be an epimorphism (consider X=∅X=\emptysetX=∅), but it is true in Set\mathrm{Set}Set if both XXX and YYY are nonempty. #40 Ah, or maybe I misunderstood what you mean by “factors through”. I couldn’t find a formal definition… I’ll elaborate on what I found and make it self-contained, including the standard definitions. (Is there a way to put diagrams in posts?)

  • Definition: a map f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y is monic if for any two i,j:A→Xi,j : A \rightarrow Xi,j:A→X with fi=fj\mathrm{fi} = \mathrm{fj}fi=fj we find i=ji = ji=j.
  • Definition: a pair (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) of maps f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y and g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z is jointly monic if for any two i,j:A→Xi,j : A \rightarrow Xi,j:A→X with fi=fj\mathrm{fi}=\mathrm{fj}fi=fj and gi=gj\mathrm{gi}=\mathrm{gj}gi=gj we find i=ji = ji=j.

  • Definition: a product of YYY and ZZZ is an object Y×ZY \times ZY×Z with projections k:Y×Z→Yk : Y \times Z \rightarrow Yk:Y×Z→Y and l:Y×Z→Zl : Y \times Z \rightarrow Zl:Y×Z→Z such that for any pair f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z there is a unique map h:X→Y×Zh : X \rightarrow Y \times Zh:X→Y×Z such that kh=f\mathrm{kh} = fkh=f and lh=g\mathrm{lh} = glh=g.

  • Theorem 1: given a pair (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) of jointly monic maps f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y and g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z, let h:X→Bh : X \rightarrow Bh:X→B be such that there exist k:B→Xk : B \rightarrow Xk:B→X and l:B→Yl : B \rightarrow Yl:B→Y with f=khf = \mathrm{kh}f=kh and g=lhg = \mathrm{lh}g=lh, then hhh is monic.

Proof: assume two i,j:A→Xi,j : A \rightarrow Xi,j:A→X such that hi=hj\mathrm{hi} = \mathrm{hj}hi=hj, then fi=khi=khj=fj\mathrm{fi} = \mathrm{khi} = \mathrm{khj} = \mathrm{fj}fi=khi=khj=fj and gi=lhi=lhj=gj\mathrm{gi} = \mathrm{lhi} = \mathrm{lhj} = \mathrm{gj}gi=lhi=lhj=gj, so by joint monicity i=ji = ji=j. Therefore, hhh is monic.

  • Theorem 2: assuming products exist, let (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) be a pair of maps f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y and g:X→Zg : X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z. Furthermore, assume that for any h:X→Bh : X \rightarrow Bh:X→B with k:B→Xk : B \rightarrow Xk:B→X and l:B→Yl : B \rightarrow Yl:B→Y such that f=khf = \mathrm{kh}f=kh and g=lhg = \mathrm{lh}g=lh we find hhh is monic. Then (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic.

Proof: Observe that in particular h:X→Y×Zh : X \rightarrow Y \times Zh:X→Y×Z is assumed to be monic, with k:X×Y→Xk : X \times Y \rightarrow Xk:X×Y→X and l:X×Y→Yl : X \times Y \rightarrow Yl:X×Y→Y the natural projections from the product. Now, let i,j:A→Xi,j : A \rightarrow Xi,j:A→X be a pair of maps such that fi=fj\mathrm{fi} = \mathrm{fj}fi=fj and gi=gj\mathrm{gi} = \mathrm{gj}gi=gj. Then by definition of product there is a unique arrow u:A→Y×Zu : A \rightarrow Y \times Zu:A→Y×Z such that ku=fi\mathrm{ku} = \mathrm{fi}ku=fi and lu=gi\mathrm{lu} = \mathrm{gi}lu=gi, as well as a unique arrow u′:A→Y×Zu' : A \rightarrow Y \times Zu′:A→Y×Z such that ku′=fj\mathrm{ku}' = \mathrm{fj}ku′=fj and lu′=gj\mathrm{lu}' = \mathrm{gj}lu′=gj. Because fi=fj\mathrm{fi} = \mathrm{fj}fi=fj and gi=gj\mathrm{gi} = \mathrm{gj}gi=gj we find u=u′u = u'u=u′, and because khi=fi\mathrm{khi} = \mathrm{fi}khi=fi and lhi=gi\mathrm{lhi} = \mathrm{gi}lhi=gi we find u=hiu = \mathrm{hi}u=hi and similarly u′=hju' = \mathrm{hj}u′=hj. Therefore, hi=hj\mathrm{hi} = \mathrm{hj}hi=hj. We assumed hhh to be monic, therefore i=ji = ji=j, which concludes the proof that (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic.

#43 Back to your definition:

Definition 2: Given a map f:X→Yf: X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a fraction of f is an epimorphism g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F such that (1) if e:X→Ze : X \rightarrow Ze:X→Z is an epimorphism such that fff and ggg both factor through it, then eee is an isomorphism; and (2) the pushout of fff and ggg is constant (factors through the terminal object).

In a category where epi+mono implies iso, this is equivalent to saying

  • Definition 2b: Given a map f:X→Yf: X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a fraction of f is an epimorphism g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F such that (1) if e:X→Ze : X \rightarrow Ze:X→Z is an epimorphism such that fff and ggg both factor through it, then eee is a monomorphism; and (2) the pushout of fff and ggg is constant (factors through the terminal object).

Which in a category where products exist comes down to

  • Definition 2c: Given a map f:X→Yf: X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y, a fraction of f is an epimorphism g:X→Fg : X \rightarrow Fg:X→F such that (1) (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is a joint morphism; and (2) the pushout of fff and ggg is constant (factors through the terminal object).

That definition is closer to my goal of treating compositions as relations between objects, and under mild conditions coincides with your intuition according to my previous post. Nice.

Now, I’ll start studying the factoring through a terminal object as a way to obtain isomorphism of fractions under reasonable conditions :-)

Technically, yes. Although that would be true regardless of which of fff or hhh is said to “factor through” the other. But if fff and hhh share a domain but not a codomain, or a codomain but not a domain, as is usually the case, then the ambiguity is resolved as only one choice is possible.

The special case when both families are single morphisms is already recorded at monomorphism#properties: if gfg fgf is a monomorphism, so is fff.

Now, I’ll start studying the factoring through a terminal object as a way to obtain isomorphism of fractions under reasonable conditions :-)

Firstly, if I’m not mistaken, using the existence of pushouts is not necessary, because the terminal object is supposed to be the pushout… so

  • Definition 2: a map g:X→Zg: X \rightarrow Zg:X→Z is a fraction of f:X→Yf : X \rightarrow Yf:X→Y if 1) (f,g)(f,g)(f,g) is jointly monic, 2) ggg is epic, and 3) for any h:Y→Ah: Y \rightarrow Ah:Y→A and k:Z→Ak : Z \rightarrow Ak:Z→A with hf=kg\mathrm{hf} = \mathrm{kg}hf=kg, we find hf\mathrm{hf}hf is constant (i.e. factors through the terminal object).

Following your idea (I think) the extension of fff and ggg into a commuting square represents the “union, closed under symmetry and transitivity” of the equivalences represented by the original maps fff and ggg. That sounds okay to me. If this union is constant, i.e. factors through the terminal object, that implies that “all information is thrown away” by the new equivalence, i.e. everything is equated.

That last part is close, but not the same I think, as my intuition that: whenever fff makes a distinction, then ggg should try to avoid making this distinction.

The tricky part is that in some categories, ggg may not be able to avoid making distinctions. In my category of choice, a terminal object exists, but nonetheless I’m not sure that ggg is free to avoid making distinctions (okay perhaps that just means the distinctions will show up in the terminal object then… true… but this is subtle). I’d have to think about quite examples for a while to make this more concrete though. Furthermore, I don’t like to have to use the terminal object as part of my definition, because I think that having a constant map implies that all information is thrown away, rather than that it is the same as saying all information is thrown away. In a sense, using the terminal object makes the definition stronger than I intend it to be.

content: #49 In general, X×XX\times XX×X being the kernel of eee is the same as saying that for any two morphisms u,vu,vu,v with codomain XXX we have eu=eve u = e veu=ev, i.e. that eee is a constant morphism in the weak sense. If eee has an image, this is the same as saying that that image is subterminal, and I think it would be better for it to be terminal. But note that at constant morphism there is given a way to phrase the strong sort of “constancy” without assuming the existence of a terminal object, so if you really happen to be in a category without a terminal object (but with pullbacks and products? I can’t think of too many categories like that) then you could use that.

What do you have against terminal objects?

It’s personal ;-) I’d rather not be dependent on them, because I have the intuition that ‘being constant’ has nothing to do with ‘being terminal’. I didn’t look it up earlier, because I simply accepted your definition of factoring through the terminal object, but your reference to constant morphism helped a lot. Why do you feel that it would be better for it to be terminal? I understand this gives you more/better properties, but I only want those properties if they also follow intuitively from what I think a fraction should be. In other words, why ask for a strong definition if the weak definition is sufficient to capture what you want? To me that goes against Occam’s razor, so to speak.

content: #51 Well, in general I believe the second stronger definition of constant is better. However, it looks like in this case I may have been led astray by that general fact, because what we’re doing is rephrasing stuff about equivalence relations in terms of their quotients, and the quotient that corresponds to the full relation is the support of an object, which is subterminal and not necessarily terminal. So in this case, I think you’re probably right to use the weaker notion.
